LoMETab: Beyond Rank-1 Ensembles
for Tabular Deep Learning

Changryeol Choi ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: CJ Logistics Email: changryeol.choi@cj.net    Hyewon Park11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: CJ Logistics Email: hyewon.park16@cj.net    Yujin Kwon Affiliation: CJ Logistics Email: yujin.kwon5@cj.net    Gowun Jeong ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: CJ Logistics Email: gowun.jeong@cj.net
Abstract

Recent tabular learning benchmarks increasingly show a tight performance cluster rather than a clear hierarchy among leading methods, spanning gradient boosted decision trees, attention-based architectures, and implicit ensembles such as TabM. As benchmark gains plateau, a complementary goal is to understand and control the mechanisms that make simple neural tabular models competitive. We propose LoMETab, a rank-rr generalization of multiplicative implicit ensembles. LoMETab lifts the rank-1 BatchEnsemble/TabM modulation to a rank-rr identity-residual Hadamard family by parameterizing each member weight as Wk=W⊙(1+Ak​Bk⊤)W_{k}=W\odot(1+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}), where WW is shared and (Ak,Bk)(A_{k},B_{k}) are member-specific low-rank factors. This exposes two practical diversity-control axes: the adapter rank rr and the initialization scale σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}, and we prove that for r≥2r\geq 2 this generalization strictly enlarges BatchEnsemble’s hypothesis class. Empirically, we show that this added capacity manifests as measurable predictive diversity after training: on representative classification datasets, LoMETab sustains higher pairwise KL than an additive low-rank ablation, and (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) provides broad control over pairwise KL, varying by up to several orders of magnitude across configurations. The induced diversity is reflected in task-appropriate output-level measures: argmax disagreement for classification and ambiguity for regression, indicating that the control extends beyond pairwise KL to decision- and output-level member variation. Finally, experiments sweeping over adapter rank rr and initialization scale σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} reveal that predictive performance is dataset-dependent over the (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) grid, supporting LoMETab as a controllable family of implicit ensembles rather than a fixed rank-1 construction.

1 Introduction

Tabular data remains one of the most prevalent data modalities in real-world applications, including finance, healthcare, and logistics. Although gradient boosted decision trees (GBDTs) remain exceptionally strong on such tasks [2, 19], deep tabular models offer a complementary advantage: their differentiable, modular backbones make it natural to incorporate learned feature embeddings, task-specific heads, auxiliary losses, and parameter-sharing mechanisms within a single end-to-end training objective. Recent benchmarks show that simple MLP-based tabular models can be surprisingly competitive, often matching or outperforming more complex attention- and retrieval-based architectures [6, 7, 16]. This makes strengthening simple neural tabular backbones a practical alternative to increasing architectural complexity.

Deep ensembles [15] are a strong way to improve such models, but training and maintaining KK independent networks scales linearly with ensemble size. Implicit ensembles reduce this cost by sharing most parameters among members while retaining member-specific perturbations. BatchEnsemble [22] assigns two learnable vectors rkr_{k} and sks_{k} to each member, which multiplicatively modulate a shared weight WW to form an effective member weight Wk=W⊙(sk​rk⊤)W_{k}=W\odot(s_{k}r_{k}^{\top}), yielding ensemble-like behavior at near single-model parameter cost. TabM [4] applies this idea to tabular MLPs, achieving performance competitive with strong tabular baselines.

However, TabM inherits the fixed rank-1 structure of BatchEnsemble: each member modulates the shared weight only through a rank-1 mask, leaving no explicit axis for increasing the capacity of member-specific modulation. Consequently, ensemble diversity—a key driver of ensemble gains—is not directly controllable; it must emerge implicitly from fixed rank-1 masks and training dynamics. Prior work also reports that BatchEnsemble members can converge to near-identical functions in some settings [23], suggesting that the rank-1 modulation may not always realize meaningful diversity.

We propose LoMETab, a rank-rr generalization of multiplicative implicit ensembles. Instead of the rank-1 BatchEnsemble mask, LoMETab assigns each member kk a low-rank adapter pair (Ak,Bk)(A_{k},B_{k}) and defines its effective weight as Wk=W⊙(1+Ak​Bk⊤)W_{k}=W\odot(1+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}). Here, Ak​Bk⊤A_{k}B_{k}^{\top} defines a rank-at-most-rr residual, and 1+Ak​Bk⊤1+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top} forms an identity-residual multiplicative perturbation of the shared weight. This Hadamard identity-residual form follows the multiplicative reparameterization used in HiRA [13], but we use it for a different purpose: member-specific diversity generation in scratch-trained tabular implicit ensembles rather than single-model fine-tuning. The resulting framework exposes the adapter rank rr and initialization scale σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} as practical axes for controlling ensemble diversity.

We first establish that the proposed rank axis genuinely expands the rank-1 design space: for r≥2r\geq 2, every BatchEnsemble mask can be represented by LoMETab structure because sk​rk⊤−𝟏s_{k}r_{k}^{\top}-\mathbf{1} has rank at most two. Thus, LoMETab strictly contains BatchEnsemble at the layer-wise effective-weight level, while the converse does not hold. Expressivity alone, however, does not guarantee meaningful ensemble diversity after training. We therefore test whether (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) yields controllable differences in member predictions, and how these axes affect performance across datasets.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We introduce LoMETab, a rank-rr multiplicative implicit-ensemble framework for tabular MLPs, where each member-specific deviation from a shared weight is parameterized by an identity-residual low-rank Hadamard perturbation. (2) We show that the added rank capacity manifests as measurable predictive diversity after training: LoMETab sustains higher pairwise KL than an additive low-rank ablation, and pairwise KL spans a wide range across the (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) grid. The same variation is reflected in argmax disagreement for classification and ambiguity for regression. (3) Across tabular benchmarks, LoMETab remains competitive with strong tabular baselines while exposing practical trade-offs among rank, ensemble size, and initialization. Tuned configurations frequently select r>1r>1 (See App. H), controlled rr- and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}-sweeps against TabM KK-scaling show dataset-dependent effects on performance.

2 Related Work

Implicit ensembles and their limitations. Implicit ensembles train a single network that internally behaves like a collection of submodels, by sharing most parameters while introducing member-specific perturbations. BatchEnsemble [22] uses rank-1 multiplicative masks, and TabM [4] adapts this idea to tabular MLPs. Other implicit-ensemble formulations diversify members through structural or activation-level variations: Masksembles [3] uses member-specific binary subnetworks, while FiLMEnsemble [21] applies member-specific feature-wise affine modulation to intermediate activations. LoMETab differs by replacing the fixed rank-1 multiplicative mask with an identity-residual low-rank multiplicative mask, making the adapter rank a tunable design axis.

Low-rank adaptation and multiplicative reparameterization. LoRA [12] introduced additive low-rank updates for parameter-efficient fine-tuning as follows: W′=W0+A​B⊤W^{\prime}=W_{0}+AB^{\top}. LoRA-Ensemble [9] uses low-rank adapters for efficient ensembles on pretrained Vision Transformers. Multiplicative low-rank reparameterizations have also been explored for single-model fine-tuning: HiRA [13] uses a Hadamard-product form W0⊙(𝟏+L1​L2)W_{0}\odot(\mathbf{1}+L_{1}L_{2}) to enable higher-rank updates. Our work adapts this multiplicative identity-residual structure from single-model fine-tuning to scratch-trained tabular implicit ensembles, where member-specific low-rank residuals are used to generate ensemble diversity.

3 Proposed Method

In this section, we present LoMETab. Sec. 3.1 fixes notation and reviews the preliminaries of our work. Sec. 3.2 defines the LoMETab layer and establishes its expressivity guarantee.

Sec. 3.3 introduces the training objective of LoMETab.

3.1 Preliminaries

Notation.

We consider an implicit ensemble with KK members indexed by k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, built on an LL-block MLP backbone indexed by l∈{1,…,L}l\in\{1,\ldots,L\}. Let hk(l−1)h_{k}^{(l-1)} denote the input representation to block ll for member kk, with hk(0)h_{k}^{(0)} being the input xx after a piecewise linear embedding layer [5]. At block ll, all members share a base weight W(l)∈ℝdout(l)×din(l)W^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}^{(l)}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}^{(l)}}, and member kk uses its own adapter parameters Ak(l),Bk(l)A_{k}^{(l)},B_{k}^{(l)} to form an effective weight Wk(l)W_{k}^{(l)}. The linear output of member kk at block ll is zk(l)z_{k}^{(l)}. The block output hk(l)h_{k}^{(l)} is obtained after the nonlinearity and dropout. After the final block, a member-specific prediction head is applied to produce o1,…,oKo_{1},\ldots,o_{K} and the final ensemble prediction y^\hat{y} is obtained by averaging the KK member predictions. When discussing a single generic layer, we omit the block index ll. We also omit bias terms for brevity; the same construction applies with or without them.

Multiplicative rank-1 implicit ensembles. BatchEnsemble [22] and TabM [4] assign each submodel two learnable adapter vectors rk∈ℝdinr_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}} and sk∈ℝdouts_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}, defining the submodel’s weight as Wk=W⊙(sk​rk⊤)W_{k}=W\odot(s_{k}r_{k}^{\top}), where ⊙\odot denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product and sk​rk⊤∈ℝdout×dins_{k}r_{k}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}} is a rank-1 multiplicative mask.

3.2 LoMETab

Formulation.

For each member kk, we assign member-specific low-rank adapter matrices Ak∈ℝdout×rA_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} and Bk∈ℝdin×rB_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times r}, so that Ak​Bk⊤A_{k}B_{k}^{\top} forms a low-rank perturbation matrix. The effective weight of member kk is defined as

Wk=W⊙(𝟏+Ak​Bk⊤).W_{k}=W\odot(\mathbf{1}+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}). (1)

Here, Ak​Bk⊤A_{k}B_{k}^{\top} is a residual with rank at most rr, and 1+Ak​Bk⊤1+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top} forms an identity-residual multiplicative perturbation of the shared weight. When Ak​Bk⊤≈0A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\approx 0, member kk remains close to the shared weight WW; larger residuals induce member-specific deviations.

Architecture.

Fig. 1 illustrates how LoMETab is inserted into a tabular MLP. A shared piecewise linear embedding [5] is applied once to the input xx and the resulting representation is copied across KK members. Each hidden linear layer is then replaced by a LoMETab Linear layer: a shared base weight WW is combined with member-specific adapters (Ak,Bk)(A_{k},B_{k}) to produce KK member-specific effective weights (Eq. (1)). The output of each member is passed through ReLU and dropout before the next block. After the final block, member-specific prediction heads produce o1,…,oKo_{1},\ldots,o_{K}, and the ensemble output is obtained by averaging member predictions.

Initialization scale.

We initialize both AkA_{k} and BkB_{k} from 𝒩⁡(0,σinit2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}^{2}). Small σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} keeps members close to the shared weight at initialization, whereas larger values induce stronger member-specific perturbations. Since the effective magnitude of Ak​Bk⊤A_{k}B_{k}^{\top} depends on both rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} under this factorization, we study them jointly as diversity-control axes in Sec. 4.3.

Expressivity hierarchy.

LoMETab is not identical to BatchEnsemble at r=1r=1 because of the identity-residual parameterization. However, for r≥2r\geq 2, any BatchEnsemble mask sk​rk⊤s_{k}r_{k}^{\top} can be represented as 1+Ak​Bk⊤1+A_{k}B_{k}\top, since sk​rk⊤−1s_{k}r_{k}^{\top}-1 has rank at most 2. Thus, the rank axis strictly enlarges the layer-wise family of representable effective weights.

Proposition 1 (Layer-wise Expressivity Hierarchy).

Fix a layer with dout,din≥2d_{\text{out}},d_{\text{in}}\geq 2 and an ensemble size K≥2K\geq 2. Define the following hypothesis classes of effective weights (W1,…,WK)(W_{1},\ldots,W_{K}):

ℋBE\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}} ={(Wk)k=1K:Wk=W⊙(skrk⊤) for some W,sk,rk},\displaystyle=\big\{(W_{k})_{k=1}^{K}:W_{k}=W\odot(s_{k}r_{k}^{\top})\text{ for some }W,s_{k},r_{k}\big\},
ℋLoMETab(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)} ={(Wk)k=1K:Wk=W⊙(𝟏+AkBk⊤) for some W,Ak,Bk}.\displaystyle=\big\{(W_{k})_{k=1}^{K}:W_{k}=W\odot(\mathbf{1}+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})\text{ for some }W,A_{k},B_{k}\big\}.

For rank r≥2r\geq 2, we have

ℋBE⊊ℋLoMETab(r).\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}}\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)}.

The proof is provided in App. A.

Remark 1.

Proposition 1 confirms that LoMETab strictly enlarges BatchEnsemble’s hypothesis class for r≥2r\geq 2. Like other implicit ensembles, LoMETab does not aim to match deep ensemble expressivity; our focus is on controllability along the rank and initialization axes.

3.3 Training Objective

Each LoMETab member receives a direct learning signal through a member-wise loss, following TabM [4]. Let ok​(x)o_{k}(x) denote the raw output of member kk after the prediction head. We optimize

ℒ⁡(x,y)=1K​∑k=1Kℓtask​(ok​(x),y),\mathcal{L}(x,y)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\ell_{\mathrm{task}}(o_{k}(x),y), (2)

where ℓtask\ell_{\mathrm{task}} is chosen according to the task type: mean squared error for regression, binary cross-entropy for binary classification, and cross-entropy for multiclass classification.

At inference time, the final prediction is obtained by averaging member predictions. For regression, we average the scalar member outputs. For classification, we first convert member outputs into predictive probabilities using sigmoid or softmax, and then average the resulting probabilities. This objective supervises each member-specific adapter directly, rather than only supervising the averaged ensemble output, allowing the parallel submodels to specialize despite sharing the backbone.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets.

For benchmark performance, we use 37 source datasets from the academic TabM benchmark: 9 Default datasets after excluding Housing (See App. B), and 28 TabZilla source datasets. The TabZilla sources are further expanded into 68 split-level evaluation tasks following the benchmark protocol; together with the 9 Default datasets, this yields 77 evaluation tasks for per-task tuning analyses. We report benchmark performance at the 37-source-dataset level and hyperparameter-selection statistics over the 77 evaluation tasks.

Baselines. We compare LoMETab against the set of methods evaluated by Gorishniy et al. [4], spanning gradient-boosted decision trees, attention- and retrieval-based deep tabular models, and MLP-based architectures including the recent implicit-ensemble baseline TabM [4]. Variants augmented with piecewise-linear embeddings [5] are marked with †\dagger, following the same convention as in TabM, while ‡\ddagger denotes the use of various periodic embeddings. To ensure a fair comparison under identical preprocessing and tuning protocols, all datasets and baseline results are sourced directly from [4]; full hyperparameter ranges and Optuna budgets are reported in App. E.

Implementation Details. The shared weight WW uses Kaiming uniform initialization [10]. Adapter initialization follows Sec. 3.2: both AkA_{k} and BkB_{k} are initialized from 𝒩⁡(0,σinit2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}^{2}). Hyperparameters— including ensemble size KK, adapter rank rr, initialization scale σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}, backbone depth LL, hidden width dd, learning rate, weight decay, and dropout —are tuned independently per dataset with up to 100 Optuna trials, and each selected configuration is evaluated across 15 random seeds. We use RMSE for regression, and Accuracy for classification. The full search space is provided in App. E.

4.2 Main Results

Fig. 2 summarizes benchmark performance over the 37 source datasets. LoMETab falls within the leading cluster of tabular methods, together with strong GBDT baselines, TabM, and recent neural tabular models. Under the adopted ranking protocol, LoMETab obtains the lowest mean rank among the compared methods: 2.1±1.32.1\pm 1.3, compared with 2.3±1.82.3\pm 1.8 for TabM (Fig. 2(a)). LoMETab also ranks ahead of strong GBDT baselines in mean rank.

The remaining panels provide a dataset-level view of this behavior. Fig. 2(b) shows that LoMETab generally improves over or remains close to the MLP reference under the sign-corrected relative metric, placing it within the top-performing group. Fig. 2(c) shows that LoMETab achieves first place on 14 datasets and ranks within the top three on 89.2% of datasets. These results establish that LoMETab is competitive across heterogeneous tabular tasks.

We emphasize that these ranks are descriptive rather than evidence of statistical dominance. As shown in Fig. 2 and observed in recent tabular benchmarks [7, 16], leading methods form a tight performance band, with small differences depending on the dataset and tuning protocol. Therefore, we use the benchmark primarily to establish that LoMETab is competitive, and focus the following analyses on the main question of this work: how the LoMETab design axes—rank rr, initialization scale σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}, and ensemble size KK—affect diversity and performance. Full per-dataset benchmark scores with standard deviations are reported in App. J.

4.3 Analyses: Controlling Predictive Diversity

Proposition 1 shows that LoMETab enlarges the rank-1 hypothesis class, but expressivity alone does not imply that the added capacity manifests as diversity among trained ensemble members. We proceed in two steps: first, we compare the multiplicative low-rank parameterization underlying LoMETab with an additive low-rank ablation; second, we test whether (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) provide effective control over ensemble diversity.

Diversity metrics.

For classification datasets, we measure (i) probabilistic diversity via symmetric pairwise Kullback–Leibler divergence between members’ predictive distributions [21], hereafter referred to as pairwise KL, and (ii) decision-level diversity via pairwise argmax disagreement [18]—the fraction of test samples on which two members predict different classes. For regression datasets, where members produce scalar predictions rather than predictive distributions, we use the Krogh–Vedelsby ambiguity [14], the average squared deviation of member predictions from the ensemble mean. We additionally report normalized ambiguity A~=A/σy2\tilde{A}=A/\sigma_{y}^{2} to enable comparison across regression tasks with different target scales. Full definitions are given in App. C.

4.3.1 Multiplicative parameterization sustains diversity.

The LoMETab layer in Eq. (1) places the member-specific low-rank residual inside a multiplicative perturbation of the shared weight. A natural ablation is an additive low-rank ensemble, Wk=W+Ak​Bk⊤W_{k}=W+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}, which uses the same adapter rank and ensemble size but does not modulate the shared weight through a Hadamard product. This comparison is not intended to exhaust all possible architectural alternatives; rather, it isolates whether the multiplicative placement of the same low-rank residual helps maintain member diversity during scratch training.

Under identical backbone, optimizer, KK, and rr, Fig. 3 shows that the additive variant rapidly reaches a low-diversity plateau, whereas LoMETab maintains substantially higher pairwise KL throughout. We refer to this persistent separation as a sustained gap. Because both variants share the same hyperparameters, the gap cannot be attributed to more members or a larger low-rank adapter. Rather, the result suggests that the placement of the low-rank factors matters for maintaining member diversity during scratch training. This is consistent with the relative-perturbation form of Eq. (1): LoMETab applies the the low-rank residual as an identity-residual multiplicative factor, W⊙(1+Ak​Bk⊤)W\odot(1+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}), whereas the additive ablation applies an absolute update Ak​Bk⊤A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}. We next study how the LoMETab axes rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} control diversity and performance.

4.3.2 Rank and initialization jointly control predictive diversity.

Grid study setup.

We sweep r∈{1,2,4,8,16}r\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} and σinit∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2,3}\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2,3\}, yielding 30 configurations per dataset. All non-swept hyperparameters are fixed to the Optuna-selected configuration for that dataset, and the ensemble size is fixed at K=32K=32. We focus on two classification datasets (adult, higgs-small) and two regression datasets (california, black-friday); full numerical grid results with seed-level standard deviations are analyzed in App. G. We interpret cells whose diversity metrics remain near the empirical floor of the grid as low-diversity regimes.

Classification diversity.

Fig. 4 shows that rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} jointly control probabilistic diversity (Fig. 4 (a-b)). At σinit=0.1\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}=0.1, rank has little effect: pairwise KL remains near the low-diversity floor on both adult (6×10−46\times 10^{-4}–9×10−49\times 10^{-4}) and higgs-small (1×10−41\times 10^{-4}–2×10−42\times 10^{-4}). As σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} increases, the rank axis becomes active. At σinit=1.0\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}=1.0, the rank sweep increases KL from about 0.0060.006 to 0.0220.022 on adult, and from about 0.0060.006 to 0.0630.063 on higgs-small. Thus, member diversity depends on the joint choice of rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}: when σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} is small, the diversity metrics remain near their empirical floor regardless of rank, whereas larger σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} makes the rank axis effective.

This probabilistic diversity is also reflected in final decisions (Fig. 4 (c)–(d)). At the smallest initialization scale (σinit=0.1\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}=0.1), pairwise argmax disagreement rate is around or below 1%1\% on both datasets. At larger scales, disagreement reaches about 55–6%6\% on adult and about 1414–17%17\% on higgs-small. Hence, (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) controls not only probability-level variation but also decision-level member variation.

Regression diversity.

Fig. 5 shows that regression follows a similar rank–scale activation pattern (Fig. 5(a, b)). At σinit=0.1\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}=0.1, normalized ambiguity remains near the metric floor for all ranks on both california and black-friday, so increasing rank alone has little effect. As σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} increases, the rank axis becomes active: at σinit=0.5\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}=0.5, ambiguity increases from roughly 0.0010.001 to 0.0160.016 on california and from about 8×10−48\times 10^{-4} to 0.0100.010 on black-friday.

Overall, regression ambiguity tends to increase with σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}, with mild saturation or non-monotonicity across rank at larger scales. Thus, (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) also controls output-level member variation for regression, but the largest-ambiguity cells do not necessarily coincide with the best RMSE.

Diversity–performance alignment.

Across Fig. 4 and Fig. 5, predictive performance broadly improves as the grid moves away from the low-σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} and low-diversity regime: classification accuracy increases in higher-diversity regions (Fig. 4 (e)–(f)), and regression RMSE generally decreases as σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} grows (Fig. 5 (c)–(d)). The trend is not strictly monotone in every cell, especially across rank and at extreme scales, but the results indicate that (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}) are useful design handles for both diversity control and dataset-dependent performance tuning.

4.4 Ablation Studies

Sec. 4.3.2 shows axis rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} jointly activate predictive diversity. We next ask whether these axes are useful for performance and calibration tuning under a controlled protocol. We conduct two single-axis sweeps on the Default benchmark datasets, comparing LoMETab against TabM KK-scaling: an rr-sweep (r∈{1,2,4,8,16}r\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}) with σinit=1.0\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}=1.0 fixed, and a σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}-sweep (σinit∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2}\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2\}) with r=16r=16 fixed. All non-swept hyperparameters are shared within each comparison, and all results are reported as sign-corrected Δ%\Delta\% relative to the TabM K=32K=32 baseline. Calibration is measured via ECE (App. C). Full results for all sweep conditions are reported in App. I.

Both rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} act as performance axes.

Tab. 1 contrasts four strategies against the (a) TabM K=32K{=}32 baseline. First, changing KK alone is not consistently beneficial under this protocol. (b) Reducing TabM to K=16K=16 yields broadly comparable results, whereas (c) increasing to K=64K=64 degrades performance on most of the datasets, which is consistent with prior observations that excessive KK may be detrimental [4]. In contrast, (d)–(e) LoMETab sweeps at K=16K{=}16 surpass or match the TabM K=32K=32 baseline on a majority of datasets by tuning either rr or σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} alone, suggesting that rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} provide useful performance tuning axes beyond changing KK alone. The strongest gains appear on CO and CH. The selected values of rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} vary across datasets, supporting our view that they should be treated as tunable design axes rather than maximized by default. Crucially, (d)–(e) often share the same gain via different selected values—for instance, CO improves by +2.6%+2.6\% through r=1r{=}1 and equally through σinit=0.3\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}{=}0.3—suggesting that the two axes provide complementary, dataset-dependent tuning effects. Where they diverge—as in CA, where the rr-sweep yields −0.8%-0.8\% while the σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}-sweep achieves +0.1%+0.1\% —the result suggests that rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} capture distinct effects, motivating joint tuning in practice.

Accuracy–Calibration trade-offs.

Tab. 2 shows that the same distinction matters for calibration. (b)–(c) Increasing KK can improve ECE on some datasets, but often at the cost of accuracy; on CO and CH, both accuracy and ECE degrade. (d)–(e) LoMETab provides additional ways to tune this trade-off through rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}: some configurations improve both accuracy and ECE on HI, OT, and CH, while CO improves substantially in accuracy (+2.6%) but worsens in ECE. This indicates that calibration is not solved by more diversity alone; the form and scale of the member deviations matter. Together, these ablations suggest that useful diversity in implicit ensembles is not just a matter of averaging more members; it also depends on how members are allowed to deviate from the shared backbone: TabM changes the number of rank-1 members through KK, whereas LoMETab changes the rank and scale of the member-specific perturbations through (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}).

5 Conclusion

We introduced LoMETab, a rank-rr multiplicative implicit ensemble that replaces the fixed rank-1 BatchEnsemble/TabM mask with an identity-residual low-rank Hadamard perturbation. This yields a strictly larger layer-wise family for r≥2r\geq 2, while exposing rr and σinit\sigma_{\mathrm{init}} as practical axes for controlling member diversity. Empirically, LoMETab remains competitive on tabular benchmarks, sustains higher pairwise KL than an additive low-rank ablation, and lets pairwise KL vary by more than two orders of magnitude, with corresponding effects on argmax disagreement, regression ambiguity, and dataset-dependent performance. These results suggest that, for tabular implicit ensembles, how members are allowed to deviate from a shared backbone is a central design question.

Limitations and Future Work.

Our analysis establishes that (r,σinit)(r,\sigma_{\text{init}}) provide two-axis control over ensemble diversity, but leaves open the question of what downstream benefits this controllability enables. Whether the diversity exposed by our formulation translates into improved uncertainty estimation or out-of-distribution detection on tabular data—tasks of increasing interest in the tabular deep learning community—is the most natural direction for future work.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 1

Notation.

We write ⊙\odot for the Hadamard (element-wise) product, ⊘\oslash for element-wise division, and 𝟏\mathbf{1} for the all-ones matrix (dimensions inferred from context). For brevity we write m:=doutm:=d_{\text{out}} and n:=dinn:=d_{\text{in}}. The hypothesis classes are:

ℋBE\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}} ={(W⊙(skrk⊤))k=1K:W∈ℝm×n,rk∈ℝn,sk∈ℝm},\displaystyle=\left\{\left(W\odot(s_{k}r_{k}^{\top})\right)_{k=1}^{K}:W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\;r_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\;s_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\right\},
ℋLoMETab(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)} ={(W⊙(𝟏+AkBk⊤))k=1K:W∈ℝm×n,Ak∈ℝm×r,Bk∈ℝn×r}.\displaystyle=\left\{\left(W\odot(\mathbf{1}+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})\right)_{k=1}^{K}:W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\;A_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\;B_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\right\}.

All shared weights WW are assumed to have non-zero entries; this is a generic condition satisfied on a full-measure subset of ℝm×n\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.

A.1 Part (a): Inclusion ℋBE⊆ℋLoMETab(r)\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)}

We first state three lemmas. Lemmas 1 and 2 are standard (see, e.g., Horn & Johnson [11]); We prove Lemmas 3 and 4, which are the key constructions.

Lemma 1 (Rank of outer product).

For any u∈ℝmu\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, rank⁡(u​v⊤)≤1\mathrm{rank}(uv^{\top})\leq 1.

Lemma 2 (Rank subadditivity).

For any X,Y∈ℝm×nX,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, rank⁡(X+Y)≤rank⁡(X)+rank⁡(Y)\mathrm{rank}(X+Y)\leq\mathrm{rank}(X)+\mathrm{rank}(Y).

Lemma 3 (Rank-ρ\rho factorization with padding).

Let r≥ρ≥0r\geq\rho\geq 0 and M∈ℝm×nM\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with rank⁡(M)=ρ\mathrm{rank}(M)=\rho. Then there exist A∈ℝm×rA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} and B∈ℝn×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} such that A​B⊤=MAB^{\top}=M.

Proof.

We proceed by case analysis on ρ\rho.

Case ρ=0\rho=0. Then M=𝟎m×nM=\mathbf{0}_{m\times n}. Setting A:=𝟎m×rA:=\mathbf{0}_{m\times r} and B:=𝟎n×rB:=\mathbf{0}_{n\times r} gives

A​B⊤=𝟎m×r⋅𝟎r×n=𝟎m×n=M.AB^{\top}=\mathbf{0}_{m\times r}\cdot\mathbf{0}_{r\times n}=\mathbf{0}_{m\times n}=M.

Case ρ≥1\rho\geq 1. By the compact SVD theorem (e.g., Horn & Johnson [11]), there exist U∈ℝm×ρU\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times\rho} with U⊤​U=IρU^{\top}U=I_{\rho}, V∈ℝn×ρV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times\rho} with V⊤​V=IρV^{\top}V=I_{\rho}, and Σ=diag⁡(σ1,…,σρ)∈ℝρ×ρ\Sigma=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{\rho})\in\mathbb{R}^{\rho\times\rho} with σi>0\sigma_{i}>0, such that

M=U​Σ​V⊤.M=U\Sigma V^{\top}.

Absorbing Σ\Sigma into UU, set U~:=U​Σ∈ℝm×ρ\tilde{U}:=U\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times\rho}, so that M=U~​V⊤M=\tilde{U}V^{\top}. Since r−ρ≥0r-\rho\geq 0, we pad with zero columns:

A:=[U~𝟎m×(r−ρ)]∈ℝm×r,B:=[V𝟎n×(r−ρ)]∈ℝn×r.A:=\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{U}&\mathbf{0}_{m\times(r-\rho)}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\qquad B:=\begin{bmatrix}V&\mathbf{0}_{n\times(r-\rho)}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}.

Writing B⊤=[V⊤𝟎(r−ρ)×n]B^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}V^{\top}\\ \mathbf{0}_{(r-\rho)\times n}\end{bmatrix} and applying block matrix multiplication,

A​B⊤=U~​V⊤+𝟎m×(r−ρ)⋅𝟎(r−ρ)×n=U~​V⊤=M.∎AB^{\top}=\tilde{U}V^{\top}+\mathbf{0}_{m\times(r-\rho)}\cdot\mathbf{0}_{(r-\rho)\times n}=\tilde{U}V^{\top}=M.\qed
Lemma 4.

For any (W1,…,WK)∈ℋBE(W_{1},\ldots,W_{K})\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}} with shared weight WW and scaling vectors sk,rks_{k},r_{k} all having nonzero entries, and for any two members i≠ji\neq j, the element-wise ratio Qi​j:=Wi⊘WjQ_{ij}:=W_{i}\oslash W_{j} satisfies rank⁡(Qi​j)≤1\mathrm{rank}(Q_{ij})\leq 1.

Proof.

By the definition of BE, Wi=W⊙(si​ri⊤)W_{i}=W\odot(s_{i}r_{i}^{\top}) and Wj=W⊙(sj​rj⊤)W_{j}=W\odot(s_{j}r_{j}^{\top}). Since WW, sjs_{j}, and rjr_{j} all have nonzero entries, Qi​jQ_{ij} is well-defined. Taking the element-wise ratio:

(Qi​j)a​b=Wa​b​(si)a​(ri)bWa​b​(sj)a​(rj)b=(si)a(sj)a⋅(ri)b(rj)b.(Q_{ij})_{ab}=\frac{W_{ab}\,(s_{i})_{a}(r_{i})_{b}}{W_{ab}\,(s_{j})_{a}(r_{j})_{b}}=\frac{(s_{i})_{a}}{(s_{j})_{a}}\cdot\frac{(r_{i})_{b}}{(r_{j})_{b}}.

Defining u∈ℝmu\in\mathbb{R}^{m} with ua=(si)a/(sj)au_{a}=(s_{i})_{a}/(s_{j})_{a} and v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with vb=(ri)b/(rj)bv_{b}=(r_{i})_{b}/(r_{j})_{b}, we have Qi​j=u​v⊤Q_{ij}=uv^{\top}, an outer product of rank at most 1. ∎

Main proof of Part (a).

Let (W1BE,…,WKBE)∈ℋBE(W_{1}^{\text{BE}},\ldots,W_{K}^{\text{BE}})\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}}. By definition, there exist W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, sk∈ℝms_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and rk∈ℝnr_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

WkBE=W⊙(skrk⊤),k=1,…,K.W_{k}^{\text{BE}}=W\odot(s_{k}r_{k}^{\top}),\quad k=1,\ldots,K.

We construct Ak,BkA_{k},B_{k} such that W⊙(𝟏+Ak​Bk⊤)=WkBEW\odot(\mathbf{1}+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})=W_{k}^{\mathrm{BE}} for each k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K.

It suffices to find AkA_{k} and BkB_{k} satisfying

Ak​Bk⊤=sk​rk⊤−𝟏,A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}=s_{k}r_{k}^{\top}-\mathbf{1}, (3)

since then W⊙(𝟏+Ak​Bk⊤)=W⊙(sk​rk⊤)=WkBEW\odot(\mathbf{1}+A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})=W\odot(s_{k}r_{k}^{\top})=W_{k}^{\text{BE}}. Let Mk:=sk​rk⊤−𝟏M_{k}:=s_{k}r_{k}^{\top}-\mathbf{1}. Since 𝟏=𝟏m​𝟏n⊤\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}_{m}\mathbf{1}_{n}^{\top}, Lemmas 1 and 2 give

ρk:=rank⁡(Mk)≤rank⁡(sk​rk⊤)+rank⁡(𝟏)≤2.\rho_{k}:=\mathrm{rank}(M_{k})\leq\mathrm{rank}(s_{k}r_{k}^{\top})+\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{1})\leq 2.

Since r≥2≥ρkr\geq 2\geq\rho_{k}, Lemma 3 yields Ak∈ℝm×rA_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} and Bk∈ℝn×rB_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} with Ak​Bk⊤=MkA_{k}B_{k}^{\top}=M_{k}, establishing (3). Since the choice of BE element was arbitrary, ℋBE⊆ℋLoMETab(r)\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)}.

A.2 Part (b): Strictness ℋLoMETab(r)⊈ℋBE\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)}\not\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}}

We exhibit an element of ℋLoMETab(r)\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)} that cannot be represented in ℋBE\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}}.

Construction of counterexample.

Let W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be any matrix with all entries nonzero, and let e1,e2∈ℝme_{1},e_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and f1,f2∈ℝnf_{1},f_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the first two standard basis vectors. Define

M1:=e1​f1⊤+e2​f2⊤,M2:=𝟎.M_{1}:=e_{1}f_{1}^{\top}+e_{2}f_{2}^{\top},\qquad M_{2}:=\mathbf{0}.

Since M1M_{1} has exactly two nonzero rows, namely f1⊤f_{1}^{\top} and f2⊤f_{2}^{\top}, which are linearly independent, rank⁡(M1)=2\mathrm{rank}(M_{1})=2. By Lemma 3, there exist A1∈ℝm×rA_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} and B1∈ℝn×rB_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} with A1​B1⊤=M1A_{1}B_{1}^{\top}=M_{1}. Set A2=𝟎A_{2}=\mathbf{0}, so that A2​B2⊤=M2=𝟎A_{2}B_{2}^{\top}=M_{2}=\mathbf{0}. Define

W1:=W⊙(𝟏+M1),W2:=W⊙(𝟏+M2)=W.W_{1}:=W\odot(\mathbf{1}+M_{1}),\qquad W_{2}:=W\odot(\mathbf{1}+M_{2})=W.

Then (W1,W2)∈ℋLoMETab(r)(W_{1},W_{2})\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{LoMETab}}^{(r)} by construction. We now show (W1,W2)∉ℋBE(W_{1},W_{2})\notin\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{BE}}.

W1=W⊙(𝟏+A1​B1⊤),W2=W⊙𝟏=W,W_{1}=W\odot(\mathbf{1}+A_{1}B_{1}^{\top}),\qquad W_{2}=W\odot\mathbf{1}=W,

and the element-wise ratio Q12:=W1⊘W2Q_{12}:=W_{1}\oslash W_{2} satisfies

(Q12)a​b={2(a,b)∈{(1,1),(2,2)},1otherwise.(Q_{12})_{ab}=\begin{cases}2&(a,b)\in\{(1,1),(2,2)\},\\ 1&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

The top-left 2×22\times 2 submatrix of Q12Q_{12} is (2112)\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\ 1&2\end{pmatrix} with determinant 3≠03\neq 0, hence rank⁡(Q12)≥2\mathrm{rank}(Q_{12})\geq 2. By the contrapositive of Lemma 4, no BE parameterization can produce the pair (W1,W2)(W_{1},W_{2}). Therefore ℋBE⊊ℋLoMETab(r)\mathcal{H}_{\text{BE}}\subsetneq\mathcal{H}_{\text{LoMETab}}^{(r)}. ∎

Appendix B Benchmark Protocol, Baseline Sourcing and Dataset Exclusion

This appendix details the benchmark protocol used in Sec. 4, including the inherited TabM pipeline, baseline result sourcing, an environment consistency check, the rationale for excluding the house dataset, and the ranking methodology.

Inherited pipeline and baseline sourcing.

Our LoMETab implementation inherits the official TabM codebase [4], which itself adopts the experimental framework of Gorishniy et al. [6]. Our implementation inherits identical dataset loaders, train/validation/test splits, preprocessing (TypedFeatureEmbeddings for categorical features, TargetScaler for regression targets), metric computation, and training protocol from this codebase. All baseline results are taken from the appendix tables of Gorishniy et al. [4] and the associated report files released in the official repository, which provides configuration and metric JSON files for all reported methods under a unified evaluation pipeline. Because LoMETab is implemented within the same forked pipeline, its results use the same data handling, preprocessing, splits, and metric computation as the released TabM benchmark artifacts; the compared baselines are taken from the corresponding published reports.

Environment consistency check.

To verify that our forked codebase preserves the evaluation environment of Gorishniy et al. [4], we reproduced the publicly released TabM configuration on the brazilian_houses dataset in our environment using 15 independent random seeds. The resulting mean test RMSE is consistent with the appendix value reported by Gorishniy et al. [4], supporting the claim that LoMETab and baseline results are evaluated under the same pipeline.

Excluded dataset: house.

During our pipeline verification, we identified a discrepancy on the house dataset. Its target distribution has median 33,200 and mean 50,074, right-skewed with the bottom 10% near 14,999—values on the order of 10410^{4}. However, RMSE values reported by prior tabular DL methods on this dataset cluster tightly around 3.0 across nearly all models, which is inconsistent with both the raw target scale and standard z-score normalization. The cause of this mismatch is unclear from publicly available materials, and to avoid potential pipeline inconsistency we exclude house from our evaluation.

Ranking methodology.

Rankings reported in Sec. 4.2 are computed from the published mean scores of each method on each dataset, following standard protocol in recent tabular DL benchmarks [6, 20]. Ties are broken by the alphabetical order of method names. We report rank distributions and paired comparisons as descriptive evidence; we do not claim statistical significance of rank differences, as seed-level raw scores are not available for all baselines.

Appendix C Diversity and Calibration Metrics: Full Definitions

We provide the full definitions of the diversity metrics used in Sec. 4.3. Throughout, KK denotes the ensemble size, NN the number of test samples, pi​(xn)p_{i}(x_{n}) the predicted class-probability vector of member ii on test sample xnx_{n}, and fi​(xn)f_{i}(x_{n}) the scalar prediction of member ii on xnx_{n}.

Pairwise KL (classification).

We measure probabilistic diversity by the symmetric pairwise Kullback–Leibler divergence between members’ predictive distributions, averaged over all member pairs and test samples:

KL=2K⁡(K−1)∑i=1K∑j=i+1K1N∑n=1N12[KL(pi(xn)∥pj(xn))+KL(pj(xn)∥pi(xn))].\mathrm{KL}=\frac{2}{K(K-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{j=i+1}^{K}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\tfrac{1}{2}\left[\mathrm{KL}(p_{i}(x_{n})\|p_{j}(x_{n}))+\mathrm{KL}(p_{j}(x_{n})\|p_{i}(x_{n}))\right]. (4)

The symmetric form ensures that the metric is invariant under the choice of reference member. Following Turkoglu et al. [21], we average over all (K2)\binom{K}{2} pairs.

Pairwise argmax disagreement (classification).

We measure decision-level diversity by the fraction of test samples on which two members predict different classes, averaged over all member pairs. Let y^i​(xn)=arg⁡maxc​pi(c)​(xn)\hat{y}_{i}(x_{n})=\arg\max_{c}p_{i}^{(c)}(x_{n}) denote the class predicted by member ii. We define

D=2K⁡(K−1)∑i=1K∑j=i+1K1N∑n=1N[y^i(xn)≠y^j(xn)],D=\frac{2}{K(K-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{j=i+1}^{K}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{i}(x_{n})\neq\hat{y}_{j}(x_{n})\right], (5)

where 𝟙​[⋅]\mathbb{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. This is the empirical pairwise disagreement rate following Nam et al. [18].

Krogh–Vedelsby ambiguity (regression).

For regression, neither pairwise KL nor argmax disagreement is defined since members produce scalar predictions rather than probability vectors. We instead use the ensemble ambiguity term from the Krogh–Vedelsby decomposition [14], defined as the average squared deviation of individual member predictions from the ensemble mean:

A=1N​K​∑n=1N∑i=1K(fi​(xn)−f¯​(xn))2,f¯​(xn)=1K​∑i=1Kfi​(xn).A=\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\left(f_{i}(x_{n})-\bar{f}(x_{n})\right)^{2},\quad\bar{f}(x_{n})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}f_{i}(x_{n}). (6)

Ambiguity is computed in the original (un-normalized) target scale.

To enable comparison across regression tasks with different target scales, we additionally report normalized ambiguity:

A~=Aσy2,\tilde{A}=\frac{A}{\sigma_{y}^{2}}, (7)

where σy2\sigma_{y}^{2} is the variance of the raw training targets.

Krogh–Vedelsby decomposition.

The ambiguity term arises naturally from the well-known decomposition of ensemble error [14]:

(f¯​(x)−y)2⏟ensemble error=1K​∑k=1K(fk​(x)−y)2⏟average member error−1K​∑k=1K(fk​(x)−f¯​(x))2⏟ambiguity.\underbrace{\bigl(\bar{f}(x)-y\bigr)^{2}}_{\text{ensemble error}}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(f_{k}(x)-y\bigr)^{2}}_{\text{average member error}}-\underbrace{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(f_{k}(x)-\bar{f}(x)\bigr)^{2}}_{\text{ambiguity}}. (8)

Hence ensemble error decreases only when the gain in ambiguity outweighs the increase in average member error—a relationship we leverage when interpreting the regression diversity–accuracy trade-off in §4.3.

Expected Calibration Error (classification).

We measure calibration quality via the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) [17], which quantifies the discrepancy between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy. For ECE, we use the ensemble-averaged predictive probability

p¯​(xn)=K−1​∑i=1Kpi​(xn).\bar{p}(x_{n})=K^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{K}p_{i}(x_{n}).

The predicted label and confidence are

y^n=arg⁡maxc​p¯(c)​(xn),confn=maxc⁡p¯(c)​(xn).\hat{y}_{n}=\arg\max_{c}\bar{p}^{(c)}(x_{n}),\qquad\mathrm{conf}_{n}=\max_{c}\bar{p}^{(c)}(x_{n}).

We partition test samples into MM equally spaced confidence bins {Bm}m=1M\{B_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} and compute

ECE=∑m=1M|Bm|Ntest​|acc⁡(Bm)−conf⁡(Bm)|,\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{|B_{m}|}{N_{\mathrm{test}}}\left|\mathrm{acc}(B_{m})-\mathrm{conf}(B_{m})\right|, (9)

where

acc(Bm)=1|Bm|∑n∈Bm𝟙[y^n=yn],conf(Bm)=1|Bm|∑n∈Bmconfn.\mathrm{acc}(B_{m})=\frac{1}{|B_{m}|}\sum_{n\in B_{m}}\mathbb{1}[\hat{y}_{n}=y_{n}],\qquad\mathrm{conf}(B_{m})=\frac{1}{|B_{m}|}\sum_{n\in B_{m}}\mathrm{conf}_{n}.

Empty bins contribute zero. We use M=15M=15 bins following Guo et al. [8]. ECE↓\downarrow indicates better calibration.

Appendix D Checklist Details

Existing assets and licenses

Our implementation builds on the official TabM codebase and benchmark artifacts released by Gorishniy et al. [4], including dataset loaders, preprocessing routines, train/validation/test splits, metric computation, hyperparameter reports, and baseline result files. The official TabM repository is released under the Apache-2.0 License. The TabZilla source datasets used by the benchmark originate from OpenML; for each dataset, we follow the original OpenML metadata, including dataset identifiers, creators, citations, and license fields. We do not redistribute raw datasets; instead, datasets are accessed through the original benchmark/OpenML pipeline. Hyperparameter optimization uses Optuna [1], which is released under the MIT License. We credit all original papers and asset owners in the relevant sections and respect the corresponding license terms.

Broader impacts

LoMETab is a general-purpose tabular learning method. Potential positive impacts include improving predictive modeling in domains where tabular data is common, such as operations, science, and business analytics. Potential negative impacts may arise if such models are deployed in high-stakes settings such as finance, healthcare, or employment without appropriate validation, fairness analysis, calibration checks, and human oversight. Our work does not directly address deployment safety or fairness, and practitioners should evaluate these aspects before deployment.

Appendix E Hyperparameter Tuning Details

This appendix provides the detailed tuning protocol for LoMETab, complementing the high-level description in Sec. 4.

Tuning framework.

We use Optuna [1] with the MedianPruner for pruning underperforming trials. The tuning objective is the validation metric: RMSE for regression (minimized), and accuracy for classification (binary and multiclass, maximized).

Trial budget.

We use up to 100 Optuna trials per (variant, dataset) combination. Exact per-dataset trial counts, which may be reduced for computationally expensive datasets, are released with our code. Each (variant, dataset) pair is tuned independently.

Search space.

The hyperparameters tuned by Optuna for the main benchmark evaluation are summarized in Table 3. This HPO space differs from the controlled sweep grids used for analysis: Sec. 4.3.2 sweeps σinit∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2,3}\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2,3\} at fixed K=32K=32, while Sec. 4.4 uses single-axis sweeps over r∈{1,2,4,8,16}r\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} and σinit∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2}\sigma_{\mathrm{init}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,1,2\}.

Training protocol.

All trials use AdamW with a batch size of 256, a maximum of 300 epochs, gradient clipping at 1.0, and mixed-precision (AMP) training. Early stopping is applied with a patience of 16 epochs on the primary validation metric.

Seed evaluation.

Once tuning completes, the Optuna-selected configuration for each (variant, dataset) pair is evaluated with 15 independent random seeds. The mean test metric across seeds is reported as the final score for that (variant, dataset) in Sec. 4.2.

Appendix F Compute Resources

Hardware and accounting scope.

All experiments were conducted on an internal on-premise GPU server equipped with a single NVIDIA H100 GPU (80GB VRAM). The reported results include both hyperparameter optimization and multi-seed evaluation across all datasets.

Compute time.

We provide a detailed breakdown of computational cost for each dataset in Tab. 4. The table reports hyperparameter tuning time, per-seed runtime (training + inference), and the number of random seeds used. This allows estimating both per-dataset and total compute requirements.

In total, hyperparameter tuning across all datasets requires approximately 64.8 GPU-hours, while multi-seed evaluation (15 seeds across 77 datasets) requires 14.1 GPU-hours, resulting in an overall compute cost of about 79.0 GPU-hours (3.3 GPU-days). In our setup, hyperparameter optimization constitutes the dominant portion of the total compute, while individual training runs are relatively lightweight. Despite evaluating multiple seeds and using an ensemble of KK submodels, the overall computational cost remains manageable due to efficient parameterization. All reported experiments correspond to the final configurations after hyperparameter search.

Appendix G Diversity Grid: Full Numerical Results

Tables 5 and 6 report the full numerical results of the diversity grid experiment summarized in Sec. 4.3.2, covering the four datasets featured in the main text. Each cell reports the mean and standard deviation over 15 seeds. Classification datasets report pairwise KL divergence, argmax disagreement, and test accuracy; regression datasets report Krogh–Vedelsby ambiguity and test RMSE. Full grid results for all remaining datasets are provided in the accompanying code repository.

Appendix H Selected Hyperparameters and Parameter Counts

Expressivity without parameter overhead.

As established in Proposition 1, LoMETab possesses a strictly larger hypothesis class than TabM; however, this increased expressivity does not necessarily entail a proportional increase in the number of parameters. While LoMETab introduces additional parameters through member-specific low-rank multiplicative factors, this increase is structurally constrained. Specifically, the adapter parameters scale as K​r​(din+dout)Kr(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}}), which is significantly smaller than the size of the full weight matrices and depends on the rank rr rather than the full model dimensionality. As a result, the additional capacity does not translate into a proportional growth in total parameter count.

Tab. 5(b) summarizes the distribution of hyperparameters across all 77 datasets, where KK denotes the number of submodels, rr the adapter rank, and σinit\sigma_{\text{init}} the initialization scale. The results show that larger ranks are frequently selected, while the ensemble size remains balanced between K=16K=16 and K=32K=32. This suggests that the additional expressivity provided by multiplicative low-rank adapters is consistently utilized across diverse datasets.

Tab. 8 further provides a detailed comparison of the selected architectures and resulting parameter counts, where dd denotes the hidden dimension and LL the number of LoMETab linear layers. Although LoMETab can in principle utilize more parameters than TabM due to its extended hypothesis class, empirical results show that this is not always the case. In practice, hyperparameter optimization naturally adjusts other architectural factors—such as dd and LL—often leading to more compact configurations.

Consequently, LoMETab does not consistently incur a higher parameter cost; instead, it frequently achieves comparable or even lower parameter counts than TabM across several datasets. This indicates that the additional expressivity introduced by the LoMETab formulation can be realized without a proportional increase in model size, highlighting a favorable trade-off between capacity and efficiency.

Appendix J Full Benchmark Results with Standard Deviations

The tables in this appendix provide the per-dataset benchmark scores used to construct Fig. 2. We follow the reporting convention of the TabM benchmark: arrows indicate whether higher or lower values are better, and the “Single model” and “Ensemble” columns correspond to the two evaluation settings reported in the released benchmark artifacts. Baseline numbers are taken from the released TabM reports, while LoMETab results are computed in our forked pipeline and averaged over 15 random seeds.

These tables are intended to make the source-dataset-level comparison transparent rather than to claim statistical dominance. In several datasets, leading methods form a tight performance band, so small gaps should be interpreted together with the reported standard deviations. A dash indicates that the corresponding benchmark report does not provide an ensemble result; nan standard deviations are inherited from the released reports when seed-level dispersion is unavailable.
